site.title: ✸ Create Your Hero — Find Your Path

header.heading: Create Your Hero
header.subtitle: Ten questions — and you'll discover which approach to self-discovery fits you best.

questions.text: When you're upset, what do you usually do first?

options.text: I tune into my body — where exactly I feel heaviness, tension, or emptiness.
I ask myself: "What does this moment tell me about my life values?"
I analyze what past situations might have triggered this reaction.
I make a list of possible actions and pick the most rational one.
I do something distracting — go for a walk, talk to a friend, make some tea.
I pray or read Scripture — it restores my sense of grounding.
I reflect that everything is from the Almighty and ease follows hardship.

questions.text: In difficult times, what gives you the most strength?

options.text: A sense that this trial has meaning, even if I can't see it yet.
Hope for relief and trust that everything is in the hands of a higher power.
The understanding that suffering is part of the human experience, and I'm not alone.
Body-based practices — breathing, movement, grounding.
A concrete action plan for the coming days.
I analyze which childhood patterns are being triggered in this situation.
I trust that things will work out — I live one day at a time.

questions.text: How do you usually handle conflict with someone close?

options.text: I focus on what I'm feeling right now and try to express it.
I try to understand the deeper reasons behind the conflict — what's really going on beneath the words.
I look for concrete agreements and steps that will improve the situation.
I reflect on forgiveness and what matters more — being right or preserving peace.
I reflect on what this conflict says about our freedom and responsibility toward each other.
I trust that time and good deeds will smooth the tension.
I pause, switch to routine tasks — let emotions cool down.

questions.text: How do you relate to your dreams?

options.text: Sometimes I write down the vivid ones — they often have a lot of bodily sensations.
I see them as reflections of unconscious processes, sometimes I try to interpret them.
If a dream repeats, I look for patterns and possible connections to ongoing tasks.
I'm drawn to dreams about death, loss, and choice — they feel especially meaningful.
Dreams are just dreams. I rarely remember them and don't attach much significance.
Sometimes dreams feel like a sign or an answer to prayer.
I see meaningful dreams as possible direction worth trusting.

questions.text: When you're angry, how exactly does it feel in your body?

options.text: Physically: fists clench, jaw tightens, heat in the chest.
Anger often comes mixed with other feelings — it's hard to isolate it.
First comes a thought about injustice, and only then a physical reaction.
I feel anger pressing against the question of patience — when to hold back and when to speak.
I feel anger pressing against the question: "What am I agreeing to that I don't want?"
I try to understand if I've crossed someone's boundary, and forgive myself.
I rarely get angry — I usually let it go before I even notice.

questions.text: How do you make important life decisions?

options.text: I listen to my inner compass — what feels right on a sensory level.
I look for signs, answers in sacred texts or in prayerful reflection.
I consult those I trust and seek wisdom in community.
I weigh pros and cons, make a list of arguments.
I trust the flow of life — if the decision is right, things will fall into place.
I explore my past decision-making patterns and their consequences.
I reflect on the finiteness of life and what truly matters.

questions.text: What does "being in control of a situation" mean to you?

options.text: The ability to stay in touch with my feelings, no matter what's happening.
Understanding the deeper motives — mine and others' — and taking them into account.
Having a clear plan and the tools to solve whatever problems come up.
Realizing that total control is impossible, and accepting that impossibility.
Doing what depends on me, and entrusting the rest.
I try not to stress — life will sort everything out on its own.
I pray for wisdom and trust that I will receive guidance.
When I can be completely honest, without fear of judgment.
When I understand the hidden reasons behind what's going on around me.
When there's a clear algorithm of action and predictable outcomes.
When I feel part of something greater than myself.
In ordinary everyday situations, among trusted people.
When I accept that nothing is guaranteed — and that's okay.
Among fellow believers, when we share common values and support.

questions.text: If you feel "stuck" in some area of life, what do you do?

options.text: I pay attention to what feelings and bodily sensations accompany this state.
I look for possible unconscious benefits of staying in this spot.
I break the big problem into small steps and start with the simplest one.
I ask myself what meaning this stuckness might hold for my path.
I pray or reflect — sometimes answers come not from the mind, but from silence.
I trust that my time hasn't come yet — everything has its season.
I try to just relax and not pressure myself — sometimes it's better to let go.

questions.text: Which type of inner questions resonates most with you?

options.text: "What am I feeling right now? Where in my body does it resonate?"
"Why do I react this way? What from childhood might have influenced it?"
"What needs to be done? What's the next step?"
"Why am I doing this? What meaning does it hold for me?"
"Is this right before God? Am I straying from the path?"
"Is this pleasing to God? How can I stay grateful?"
"Am I doing everything right? Is it time for a change?"

C.title: THE STRATEGIST
C.description: You think clearly and step by step. For you, problems are tasks with solutions, and you know how to tackle them. Plans and algorithms are your element.

P.title: SHADOW ARCHAEOLOGIST
P.description: You seek depth and cause. You're curious about where things come from, and you're willing to dig into the past to understand the present. Unconscious scripts aren't an abstraction to you — they're a field for exploration.

G.title: THE FEELING BLADE
G.description: You trust your body and the moment. You care about what's happening right now, and you know how to listen to your sensations. Pausing and feeling is your greatest resource.

E.title: WANDERER WITHOUT A MAP
E.description: You ask the big questions. Meaning, freedom, solitude — these aren't abstractions to you, they're what you deal with every day. You're not looking for ready-made answers — you're looking for your own path.

S.title: THE SELF-GUIDED WAYFARER
S.description: You already have your own resources and ways of coping. Perhaps books, practices, or support from loved ones are enough. You're already moving along your own path.

X.title: PILGRIM OF LIGHT
X.description: You seek grounding in faith and see meaning in trials. For you, self-discovery is inseparable from your relationship with God. Scripture and prayer are your guides, and community is your support on the journey.

I.title: SEEKER OF THE STRAIGHT PATH
I.description: You seek balance between trust in the Almighty and your own effort. Patience, gratitude, and justice aren't just words — they're daily practice. Spiritual reflection is your source of direction.

howToUseList: Look for a specialist or guide who works in an approach close to you
Pay attention to which questions and techniques resonate with you
Use the strengths of your profile in everyday life
Remember: there is no perfect approach — what matters most is trust

recommendations.C: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy may suit you well. It provides concrete tools for working with thoughts and behaviors. You'll be able to set clear goals and track your progress.
recommendations.P: Psychoanalytic therapy may resonate with you. You'll be able to explore the deeper causes of your experiences, understand unconscious scripts, and work with recurring patterns.
recommendations.G: Gestalt therapy will help you develop contact with your body and the present moment. You'll learn to complete unfinished situations, express feelings, and find resources in the here and now.
recommendations.E: Existential therapy offers a space to explore fundamental questions: meaning, freedom, solitude, death. You'll be able to find your own answers.
recommendations.S: You may not need formal therapy right now. You already have your own resources and ways of coping. If you ever want to deepen your self-knowledge — you can always come back.
recommendations.X: Christian spiritual guidance may be your path. A conversation with a priest, spiritual director, or Christian counselor can help you connect self-discovery with faith, and Scripture with daily life.
recommendations.I: Islamic spiritual guidance may be your direction. A conversation with an imam or Muslim counselor can help you find balance between tawakkul and personal effort, and deepen your connection with the Almighty.

footer.disclaimer: This quiz is a self-exploration tool, not a professional diagnosis. It can help you orient yourself, but it does not replace working with a specialist.
footer.helpText: If you're struggling, having suicidal thoughts, or feel like you can't cope — please reach out to a professional. Call 988 (US) or your local crisis line.
